RagShortTexts: Situated across critical crossroads, Hibernians maintained fortified border networks anchored against rivers, mountain passes, and dense forests.
Under intense pressure from migrating populations and rival expansion, the borders faced acute strain from regional upheavals.
Frontier governors exercised broad emergency prerogatives, maintaining patrol outposts and garrison bastions to shield agrarian heartlands.

Variants.Content: The territorial perimeter of Hibernians spanned treacherous terrain encompassing river crossings, mountain defiles, and primeval woodlands. Shielding the arterial supply corridors leading toward Hill of Tara & Gaelic Tuaths, the regime garrisoned fortified outposts and watchtowers tasked with round-the-clock reconnaissance. In 374 AD, strategic volatility reached a fever pitch, aggravated by border clashes and cross-frontier raiding. Provincial commanders operated under persistent resource deficits, forced to contain covert banditry while preparing against full-scale royal invasions, knowing that any fatal rupture along the forward limes would unleash catastrophic devastation upon undefended inland communities.

Atop the hilltop watch post, the sentry counts smoke on the northern moors and watches for boats on the sea. Raiders have come twice this season, and the chieftain orders a fire lit only when the enemy is certain to be seen. The men sleep in their cloaks beside their spears, ready to run to the coast at the first signal.

His foster son rides north with gifts for a rival king, a bond the chieftain hopes will keep the raids in check. Hostages from three tuaths sit in his hall, and their families send tribute on time only while their sons are safe. A breach on the border would cost him the hostages as well as the herds.
